subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 9! In this unit you will learn about probability – the branch of mathematics that measures how likely things are to happen. Probability is all around you, every single day. When you glance at the sky before walking to the masjid and judge whether it might rain, when Hassan wonders whether his football team will win on Friday, or when Amina flips a bottle cap to decide who goes first in a game, you are all thinking about chance. This unit gives you the mathematical tools to describe that chance precisely, instead of only guessing.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 6 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Describe the likelihood of events using words such as impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely and certain.
Place events on a probability scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
Calculate the probability of an event using the formula favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
Express any probability as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage, and convert between them.
List all the possible outcomes of a situation in an organised way.
Use the idea of complementary events – that P(event) + P(not event) = 1.
Run probability experiments, record results in tally and frequency tables, and find experimental probability.

concepts.title: The Language of Likelihood
concepts.explanation:
Before we reach numbers, we describe chance with words. Every event in the world sits somewhere between two extremes. Some things are impossible – they simply cannot happen. Some are certain – they are sure to happen. Most events fall somewhere in between, and we describe them with words such as unlikely, even chance and likely.

Think about these everyday situations. It is certain that the sun will set this evening and certain that you will breathe in the next minute. It is impossible to roll an 8 on an ordinary die numbered 1 to 6, and impossible to travel back to yesterday. It is very likely that a classmate at Nuur Academy is wearing shoes today. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that it snows in the desert. And when Yusuf tosses a fair coin, there is an even chance it lands heads.

We can arrange these words on a likelihood scale that runs from left to right, from impossible to certain:

Impossible → Unlikely → Even chance → Likely → Certain

Underneath the words we can imagine a number line: impossible is at one end, certain is at the far end, and even chance sits exactly in the middle. This picture is one of the most useful ideas in the whole unit, because it lets us line up events and compare their chances at a glance. An event that is 'likely' sits further along the scale than one that is only 'unlikely', so it has a greater chance of happening.
concepts.example: A word of caution that catches many learners: likely does not mean certain. If an event is likely, it will *probably* happen – but it might not. Rain is likely on a heavy, grey morning, yet the day can still stay dry. In the same way, unlikely does not mean impossible. An unlikely event has a small chance, but a small chance is still a chance. Keeping these differences straight is the first step to thinking clearly about probability.

concepts.title: The Probability Scale from 0 to 1
concepts.explanation:
Words are useful, but they are not precise. Two people might disagree about whether an event is 'likely' or only 'quite likely'. To be exact, mathematicians turn likelihood into a number. Every probability is a number between 0 and 1:

A probability of 0 means the event is impossible – it never happens.

A probability of 1 means the event is certain – it always happens.

A probability of 1/2 (that is 0.5, or 50%) means an even chance.

The closer a probability is to 1, the more likely the event.

The closer a probability is to 0, the less likely the event.

No probability can ever be less than 0 or greater than 1. If you ever calculate a probability of 2, or of −0.3, you know at once that a mistake has crept in. This is a wonderful checking tool: a sensible answer always sits between 0 and 1. We can match the number scale to the word scale like this: 0 is impossible, about 0.25 is unlikely, 0.5 is an even chance, about 0.75 is likely, and 1 is certain.

The same probability can be written in three different forms, and all three mean exactly the same thing. An even chance is 1/2 as a fraction, 0.5 as a decimal, and 50% as a percentage. Being able to switch between these forms is one of the key skills of this unit. To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the top by the bottom. To turn a decimal into a percentage, multiply by 100. So 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, and 3/4 = 0.75 = 75%.
concepts.example: Consider the weather forecast, which you have surely heard on the radio. When the forecaster says there is a 30% chance of rain, they are giving a probability in percentage form. It means that out of 100 days with these same conditions, rain would fall on about 30 of them. It also tells us the chance of no rain is 70%, because the two must add up to 100%. Notice how the number 30% is far more useful than simply saying 'it might rain' – it tells you *how much* it might rain, so you can decide whether to carry a covering for the walk to Dhuhr prayer.

concepts.title: Calculating Probability
concepts.explanation:
Now we come to the heart of the unit: how to *work out* a probability. When every outcome is equally likely, we use one simple formula:

Probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes

A favourable outcome is simply an outcome that counts as the event we want – the word does not mean 'good', it just means 'the ones we are counting'. Let us see the formula in action with a fair coin. A coin has 2 equally likely outcomes: heads or tails. Only 1 of them is heads. So the probability of heads is 1 out of 2 = 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. In the same way, the probability of tails is also 1/2.

Now take an ordinary die numbered 1 to 6. There are 6 equally likely outcomes. The probability of rolling a 3 is 1 out of 6 = 1/6, which is about 0.167 or 16.7%. What about rolling an even number? The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6 – that is 3 favourable outcomes out of 6 – so the probability is 3/6 = 1/2 = 50%. Rolling a number less than 4 means getting 1, 2 or 3, again 3 outcomes out of 6, so once more the probability is 1/2. Always ask two questions: how many outcomes count as my event, and how many outcomes are there altogether?

Here is an example with objects. Imagine a bag holding coloured beads, the kind Khadija sews onto cloth: 8 red beads and 4 blue beads, so 12 beads in total. If she draws one without looking, the probability of red is 8/12, which simplifies to 2/3. The probability of blue is 4/12 = 1/3. Notice that these two fractions add up to 2/3 + 1/3 = 1, because the bead must be either red or blue – there is no other possibility. Always simplify your probability fractions to their lowest terms, just as you learned in the fractions unit, because 2/3 is much clearer than 8/12.
concepts.example: Let us try one more, with cards numbered like a market game. Suppose you have five cards showing 1, 1, 2, 3, 4. There are 5 cards in total. Because there are two cards showing '1', the probability of drawing a 1 is 2/5 = 0.4 = 40%. The probability of drawing a 2 is 1/5 = 20%, since only one card shows a 2. The probability of drawing a number greater than 2 means drawing the 3 or the 4, which is 2/5 = 40%. Working carefully through each event like this is exactly how a mathematician thinks.

concepts.title: Listing Outcomes and Complementary Events
concepts.explanation:
To calculate a probability correctly, you must be sure you have counted all the possible outcomes – missing even one will spoil your answer. For simple situations we list the outcomes in an organised way. The outcomes of tossing a coin are just {heads, tails}. The outcomes of rolling a die are {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}. Writing them out, especially in order, makes sure none are forgotten and none are counted twice.

When two things happen together, we list every combination. Suppose Omar tosses a coin and rolls a die at the same time. We can pair each coin result with each die result. With heads there are six pairs: (H,1), (H,2), (H,3), (H,4), (H,5), (H,6). With tails there are six more: (T,1), (T,2), (T,3), (T,4), (T,5), (T,6). That gives 12 outcomes in total. Now probabilities are easy: the probability of 'heads and a 6' is just 1/12, because only one of the twelve pairs matches. The probability of 'tails and an even number' is 3/12 = 1/4, since (T,2), (T,4) and (T,6) all match. Organised listing turns a tricky question into simple counting.

A second powerful idea is the complement. The complement of an event is the event not happening. Because something either happens or it does not, these two probabilities must always add up to 1:

P(event) + P(not event) = 1, which rearranges to P(not event) = 1 − P(event).
concepts.example: This is a great shortcut. On a die, the probability of rolling a 6 is 1/6, so the probability of not rolling a 6 is 1 − 1/6 = 5/6. You did not have to count all five other faces; you simply subtracted from 1. If the probability that Hassan's bus arrives on time is 0.85, then the probability it does not arrive on time is 1 − 0.85 = 0.15. Whenever a question asks for the chance that something does *not* happen, think of the complement first – it is often the quickest path to the answer.

concepts.title: Theoretical and Experimental Probability
concepts.explanation:
There are two ways to find a probability, and it is vital to tell them apart. Theoretical probability is what the mathematics *predicts* should happen, worked out with the formula. Experimental probability is what *actually* happens when you carry out a real experiment and count the results.

For a fair coin the theoretical probability of heads is 1/2, so we expect heads about half the time. But suppose Amina actually flips a coin 20 times and records the outcomes. She counts 12 heads and 8 tails. Her experimental probability of heads is 12/20 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%, and of tails 8/20 = 40%. The experimental result (60%) is not the same as the theoretical prediction (50%) – there is a gap of 10%. This does not mean the coin is faulty or the maths is wrong. It is completely normal.

Why do the two differ? Because of random variation. In a small number of trials, chance naturally causes the results to wobble above and below the predicted value. If you flip a coin only ten times you might easily get 7 heads, which is 70%, far from 50%. This wobble is the nature of chance itself.

But something remarkable happens as you do more trials. The experimental probability creeps closer and closer to the theoretical value. This is called the Law of Large Numbers. Look at how the results settle down for a fair coin:

10 flips: you might get 7 heads → 70%, quite far from 50%.

100 flips: you might get 53 heads → 53%, closer.

1000 flips: you might get 501 heads → 50.1%, closer still.

10 000 flips: you might get 5003 heads → 50.03%, very close indeed.
concepts.example: This is why more trials give more reliable results, and it is the reason insurance companies and scientists trust probability: over very many events, the wobble shrinks and the outcome becomes predictable. When you run your own experiments in this unit, do as many trials as you can, and record them in a tally chart so you never lose count. A running table – trial number, outcome, running totals – lets you watch the experimental probability settle towards the theoretical one before your eyes.

concepts.title: Fairness, Games and Real-World Probability
concepts.explanation:
A game is fair when every player has an equal chance of winning. Probability lets us test fairness with mathematics instead of arguing about it. If Farah and Idris play a game where Farah wins by rolling an even number and Idris wins by rolling an odd number, the game is fair, because P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2 and P(odd) = 3/6 = 1/2 – both have an equal chance. But if Farah won on 'a number greater than 2' (that is 3, 4, 5 or 6, a probability of 4/6) while Idris won on '1 or 2' (a probability of only 2/6), the game would be unfair in Farah's favour. To make it fair again, we would change the rules until each player's probability is equal.

Probability guides important decisions far beyond games. Consider quality control in a factory. Suppose a workshop tests 100 water pumps and finds that 3 are faulty. The probability that a pump is faulty is 3/100 = 3%, and the probability it works is 97/100 = 97%. If that faulty rate climbs above an agreed limit, the manager knows to stop and investigate. In the same way, a shop that receives 500 solar lamps, knowing 3 in every 100 are usually faulty, can expect about 500 × 3/100 = 15 faulty lamps, and can plan for that.

Probability also shapes sport. If a footballer scores from 7 of her last 10 penalty kicks, her experimental probability of scoring is 7/10 = 70%, and we might predict she will score about 70% of her future penalties. It shapes weather planning, where a 20% chance of rain over the next few days helps a farmer near Kismaayo decide when to harvest. And it lies behind insurance and medicine, where experts weigh the probability of events to keep people safe. In every case, the same simple idea is at work: count the favourable outcomes, divide by the total, and reason carefully about what the number means.

You have now met six big ideas: the language of likelihood, the probability scale from 0 to 1, calculating probability with the formula, listing outcomes and using complements, the difference between theoretical and experimental probability, and applying all of this to fairness and the real world. These ideas are not separate – they weave together. When you judge whether a game is fair, you list the outcomes, calculate each player's probability as a fraction, perhaps convert it to a percentage to compare, and reason about the complement to check your total comes to 1.
concepts.example: The best way to lock these ideas into memory is to use them with real objects around your home. Flip a bottle cap fifty times and tally the results. Draw beans of two colours from a cup and predict, then test, the probability of each. Estimate the chance of rain before you set out, then see what actually happens. Every time you reason about chance, your understanding grows stronger, and the statistics you will meet in later years will feel familiar and friendly. Now let us practise together with some fully worked examples.

methods.title: How to calculate a probability
methods.example: A bag contains 5 red beads, 3 blue beads and 2 green beads. One bead is drawn at random. Find P(red), P(blue) and P(not green).
steps: Count the total number of equally likely outcomes.
Count how many outcomes are favourable (count as your event).
Write favourable over total as a fraction.
Simplify the fraction, and convert to a decimal or percentage if asked.

methods.title: How to find experimental probability
methods.example: What is the probability of rolling an even number on an ordinary die? Give your answer as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
steps: Run the experiment many times and tally the results.
Count how many times your event happened.
Divide by the total number of trials.
Compare with the theoretical probability — more trials means closer agreement.

methods.title: How to check a game is fair
methods.example: The probability that Zahra's team wins is 3/4. Write this as a decimal and a percentage, and find the probability that they do not win.
steps: List each player's winning outcomes.
Work out each player's probability of winning.
If the probabilities are equal, the game is fair.
If not, change the rules until each player's probability is equal.

methods.title: Listing outcomes for two events
methods.example: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. List all the outcomes, then find P(heads and an even number).
steps: Pair each coin result with each die result: (H,1), (H,2), (H,3), (H,4), (H,5), (H,6), (T,1), (T,2), (T,3), (T,4), (T,5), (T,6) – that is 12 outcomes.
'Heads and even' means (H,2), (H,4), (H,6), which is 3 outcomes.

methods.title: Experimental probability
methods.example: Maryam rolls a die 60 times. The number 2 comes up 12 times. Compare the experimental probability of rolling a 2 with the theoretical probability.
steps: Experimental probability = 12/60 = 1/5 = 20%.
Theoretical probability = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%.
They are close but not equal.
The difference is due to random variation, and with more rolls the experimental value would drift nearer to 1/6.

methods.title: Expected number from a percentage
methods.example: A quality check shows 3 out of every 100 lamps are faulty. A shop in Mombasa receives 500 lamps. How many would you expect to be faulty, and what is the probability a lamp works?
steps: Expected faulty = 500 × 3/100 = 15 lamps.
The probability a lamp works is the complement: 1 − 3/100 = 97/100 = 97%.
So about 485 lamps should work properly.
State your final answer clearly, including the expected count and the probability.

workedExamples.title: A probability from a bag
workedExamples.prompt: A bag contains 5 red beads, 3 blue beads and 2 green beads. One bead is drawn at random. Find P(red), P(blue) and P(not green).
workedExamples.solution: First find the total: 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 beads. P(red) = 5/10 = 1/2. P(blue) = 3/10. For P(not green), use the complement: P(green) = 2/10 = 1/5, so P(not green) = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5. Notice we could also add red and blue directly: 5/10 + 3/10 = 8/10 = 4/5, which agrees — a good check.

workedExamples.title: Even number on a die
workedExamples.prompt: What is the probability of rolling an even number on an ordinary die? Give your answer as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
workedExamples.solution: The even outcomes are 2, 4 and 6, so there are 3 favourable outcomes out of 6 total. P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2. As a decimal, 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. As a percentage, 0.5 × 100 = 50%. All three forms describe the same even chance.

workedExamples.title: Converting between forms
workedExamples.prompt: The probability that Zahra's team wins is 3/4. Write this as a decimal and a percentage, and find the probability that they do not win.
workedExamples.solution: 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75, and 0.75 × 100 = 75%. The probability they do not win is the complement: 1 − 3/4 = 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. Winning is 'likely'; not winning is 'unlikely'.

workedExamples.title: Listing outcomes for two events
workedExamples.prompt: A coin is tossed and a die is rolled. List all the outcomes, then find P(heads and an even number).
workedExamples.solution: Pair each coin result with each die result: (H,1), (H,2), (H,3), (H,4), (H,5), (H,6), (T,1), (T,2), (T,3), (T,4), (T,5), (T,6) – that is 12 outcomes. 'Heads and even' means (H,2), (H,4), (H,6), which is 3 outcomes. So P = 3/12 = 1/4.

workedExamples.title: Experimental probability
workedExamples.prompt: Maryam rolls a die 60 times. The number 2 comes up 12 times. Compare the experimental probability of rolling a 2 with the theoretical probability.
workedExamples.solution: Experimental probability = 12/60 = 1/5 = 20%. Theoretical probability = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%. They are close but not equal. The difference is due to random variation, and with more rolls the experimental value would drift nearer to 1/6.

workedExamples.title: Expected number from a percentage
workedExamples.prompt: A quality check shows 3 out of every 100 lamps are faulty. A shop in Mombasa receives 500 lamps. How many would you expect to be faulty, and what is the probability a lamp works?
workedExamples.solution: Expected faulty = 500 × 3/100 = 15 lamps. The probability a lamp works is the complement: 1 − 3/100 = 97/100 = 97%. So about 485 lamps should work properly.

workedExamples.title: Is the game fair?
workedExamples.prompt: In a spinner game, Aisha wins on red and Ibrahim wins on blue. The spinner has 8 equal sections: 3 red, 3 blue and 2 yellow (yellow means no one wins). Is the game fair?
workedExamples.solution: P(red) = 3/8 and P(blue) = 3/8. Because both players have the same probability of 3/8, the game is fair, even though the 2 yellow sections mean neither player wins on a quarter of the spins.

workedExamples.title: Choosing from survey data
workedExamples.prompt: In a survey of 200 students, 60 chose science and 40 chose English as their favourite subject. What is the probability a randomly chosen student prefers science or English?
workedExamples.solution: Favourable = 60 + 40 = 100 students out of 200. P(science or English) = 100/200 = 1/2 = 50%. Because these choices cannot both be a single student's favourite, we simply add them.

activities.title: The 50-Flip Coin Experiment
activities.materials: a coin or a bottle cap, paper, a pencil.
steps: Predict: how many heads do you expect in 50 flips? (Use the theoretical probability of 1/2.)
Flip the coin 50 times, marking a tally for heads and tails as you go.
Count your tallies and write the experimental probability of heads as a fraction and a percentage.
Compare your result with your prediction of 25 heads. How close were you? Why is it rarely exactly 25?
Keep your tally chart – it shows the Law of Large Numbers in action.

activities.title: Bag of Beans Probability
activities.materials: a cup or bag, and beans, stones or beads in two colours (for example 6 dark and 4 light).
steps: Count your beans and write the theoretical probability of drawing each colour.
Without looking, draw one bean, record its colour, then put it back and shake.
Repeat 30 times, keeping a tally for each colour.
Work out the experimental probability of each colour and compare it with your prediction.

activities.title: Design a Fair Spinner (Maths Game)
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, a ruler, and a paper clip to spin around a pencil point.
steps: Draw a circle and divide it into equal sections – try 4, 6 or 8.
Colour the sections so a two-player game is fair (each player wins on an equal number of sections).
Write each player's probability of winning to prove the game is fair.
Now redesign it to be deliberately UNFAIR, and calculate how unfair it is.
This activity shows how probability decides fairness in every game you play.

activities.title: The Two-Dice Investigation
activities.materials: two dice (or number cards 1–6 drawn twice), paper, a pencil.
steps: List every possible total when two dice are added (the smallest is 2, the largest is 12).
Predict which total you think will come up most often, and why.
Roll the two die 40 times and tally each total.
Which total appeared most? Investigate why 7 has more ways of being made than 2 or 12.

activities.title: Family Weather Forecast Tracker
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, and one week of patience.
steps: Each morning, ask your family to predict the chance of rain as a percentage (or make your own prediction, or ask your AI tutor, if no one else is available).
Write down everyone's prediction and note whether it actually rains.
After a week, work out how often the family predictions matched reality.
Discuss: does a 30% chance of rain mean it will not rain? Talk about what the percentage really means.

activities.title: Probability Word Wall (Group Task)
activities.materials: paper cards, a pencil, and one or more friends or family members (or your AI tutor if no one else is available).
steps: On each card write one probability word: impossible, unlikely, even chance, likely, certain.
Take turns calling out an everyday event (for example, 'the sun rises tomorrow').
Everyone holds up the card they think fits, then discuss any disagreements.
Keep score of who reasons most clearly – explaining WHY matters more than being fast.

After your activities, talk or write about these questions: Which activity helped you understand chance best? Did any experiment surprise you by not matching the theoretical probability? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Key rule 1
rules.text: The Probability Formula Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. Every probability is between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%). 0 = impossible, one half = even chance, 1 = certain.

rules.title: Complement Rule
rules.text: P(event) + P(not event) = 1. So P(not event) = 1 − P(event). Use it whenever a question asks for the chance something does NOT happen.

rules.title: Three Forms Rule
rules.text: The same probability can be a fraction, a decimal or a percentage. Fraction to decimal: divide top by bottom. Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: a) 1/2 = 50%, b) 32/50 = 16/25 = 64%, c) difference is random variation in a small sample of 50 flips.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A spinner has 4 equal sections: red, blue, green, yellow. You spin it twice. a) Find P(red both times). b) Find P(the same colour both times).
A factory sample of 500 bulbs has 475 working, 20 dim and 5 dead. Find a) P(works perfectly) b) P(some problem: dim or dead).
Explain the key idea in Theoretical and Experimental Probability.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
There are two ways to find a probability, and it is vital to tell them apart. Theoretical probability is what the mathematics *predicts* should happen, worked out with the formula. Experimental probability is what *actually* happens when you carry out a real experiment and count the results.

For a fair coin the theoretical probability of heads is 1/2, so we expect heads about half the time. But suppose Amina actually flips a coin 20 times and records the outcomes. She counts 12 heads and 8 tails. Her experimental probability of heads is 12/20 = 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%, and of tails 8/20 = 40%. The experimental result (60%) is not the same as the theoretical prediction (50%) – there is a gap of 10%. This does not mean the coin is faulty or the maths is wrong. It is completely normal.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Fairness, Games and Real-World Probability.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A game is fair when every player has an equal chance of winning. Probability lets us test fairness with mathematics instead of arguing about it. If Farah and Idris play a game where Farah wins by rolling an even number and Idris wins by rolling an odd number, the game is fair, because P(even) = 3/6 = 1/2 and P(odd) = 3/6 = 1/2 – both have an equal chance. But if Farah won on 'a number greater than 2' (that is 3, 4, 5 or 6, a probability of 4/6) while Idris won on '1 or 2' (a probability of only 2/6), the game would be unfair in Farah's favour. To make it fair again, we would change the rules until each player's probability is equal.

I can express any probability as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage, and convert between them.
I can list all the possible outcomes of a situation in an organised way.
I can use the idea of complementary events – that P(event) + P(not event) = 1.
I can run probability experiments, record results in tally and frequency tables, and find experimental probability.
